title: Search systems
scopeHtml: Scope: inverted index, Elasticsearch/Lucene, relevance, indexing pipelines.

notes.title: Why databases are bad at search
notes.html:
Text search asks "which documents contain these words, best matches first". A relational database with LIKE '%shoes%' has to scan every row, because a B-tree index sorts whole values and cannot help with a middle-of-string match. On 100M product rows that is seconds to minutes per query.

A search system flips the structure so lookup by word is instant, adds language handling (stemming, synonyms, typos) and ranks results by relevance.

Worked example. 50M product titles. SELECT ... WHERE title ILIKE '%running shoes%' scans about 5 GB of text: roughly 5 to 20 s. Elasticsearch on the same data: 10 to 50 ms.

Postgres has basic full-text search (tsvector, GIN index) which is a good first step under a few million documents; it lacks easy distributed scaling, rich relevance tuning and facets.

Industry examples. Amazon and Flipkart product search, GitHub code search, Uber Eats restaurant search, Swiggy dish search, Slack message search; Wikipedia uses Elasticsearch (previously Lucene-based).

Everyday analogy. The index at the back of a book: instead of reading every page to find "photosynthesis", you look it up alphabetically and get page numbers.

Common interview traps.

  • Proposing LIKE '%x%' or regex for search at scale.
  • Treating the search engine as the primary database of record.

notes.title: The inverted index
notes.html:
An inverted index maps each term to the list of documents containing it (a posting list). Building it is the heart of Lucene, Elasticsearch, Solr and OpenSearch.

Steps (analysis pipeline) for each document:

  1. Tokenize: split text into words. "Red running-shoes!" -> red, running, shoes.
  2. Normalize: lowercase, strip accents, remove punctuation.
  3. Stop words (optional): drop "the", "a" (modern engines often keep them).
  4. Stem or lemmatize: running -> run, shoes -> shoe.
  5. Synonyms (optional): sneakers = shoes.
  6. Store term -> sorted list of (docId, term frequency, positions).
Doc1: "red running shoes"
Doc2: "blue running shirt"
Doc3: "red shirt"

Term     Postings (docId : positions)
red      1:[0]  3:[0]
run      1:[1]  2:[1]
shoe     1:[2]
blue     2:[0]
shirt    2:[2]  3:[1]

Query "red AND shirt": postings(red) = {1,3}, postings(shirt) = {2,3} -> intersect = {3}

Intersection of sorted lists is fast (merge walk, skip lists, bitmaps). Phrase queries use positions ("running shoes" needs run at p and shoe at p+1).

Lucene internals worth knowing.

  • The index is split into immutable segments. New documents go into an in-memory buffer, flushed to a new small segment. Segments are never edited; deletes are marked in a bitset and removed during merges (background compaction of many small segments into fewer big ones).
  • Posting lists are compressed (delta encoding plus bit-packing, frame of reference).
  • A term dictionary uses an FST (finite state transducer) held in memory for prefix lookups.
  • Doc values (column-oriented) support sorting and aggregations; stored fields keep the original _source.

Worked example. 10M docs, vocabulary 2M terms. Posting list for "the" has 9M entries; compressed delta ids at about 1 byte each is about 9 MB. A query for rare term "kubernetes" touches a list of 40k entries, tiny. Cost depends on posting-list length, which is why rare terms are cheap and common terms are expensive.

Decision gravity. Choosing the analyzer is nearly a one-way door: changing it needs a full reindex because tokens are baked into the index at write time. Design analyzers (language, synonyms, edge n-grams for autocomplete) before loading hundreds of millions of documents.

Industry examples. Apache Lucene is the library under Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Solr and (a variant of its ideas) many others; Tantivy (Rust) and Bleve (Go) are Lucene-like; Postgres GIN is an inverted index too.

Everyday analogy. The book index again: word to pages. Building it is expensive once; looking up is cheap forever.

Common interview traps.

  • Using different analyzers at index time and query time and wondering why nothing matches.
  • Thinking updates are in-place; they are delete plus insert of a whole document.
  • Forgetting that stemming changes meaning ("university" vs "universe" in aggressive stemmers).

notes.title: Relevance ranking: TF-IDF and BM25
notes.html:
Finding matching documents is easy; ordering them is where search quality lives.

Intuition:

  • Term frequency (TF): a doc mentioning "shoe" 5 times is more about shoes than one mentioning it once, but with diminishing returns.
  • Inverse document frequency (IDF): rare words matter more. "the" appears everywhere (useless), "gore-tex" is rare (informative).
  • Field length normalization: a match in a 3-word title beats the same match in a 3,000-word description.

BM25 (default in Lucene since version 6 / Elasticsearch 5) refines TF-IDF with saturating TF and length normalization:

score(q,d) = sum over terms t: IDF(t) * (tf * (k1 + 1)) / (tf + k1 * (1 - b + b * len/avglen))

Defaults: k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75. Raising k1 makes repeated terms matter longer; b=0 disables length normalization.

Beyond text score, real search blends many signals:

  • Field boosts: title^3, brand^2, description^1.
  • Business signals: popularity, rating, recency, price, in-stock, personalization.
  • Function score / rescoring: run cheap retrieval for the top 1,000, then rerank the top 100 with an expensive model (learning to rank, LambdaMART, neural cross-encoders).
  • Semantic / vector search: embed queries and docs, find nearest neighbours (HNSW indexes, Elasticsearch dense_vector, OpenSearch k-NN, pgvector), often hybrid with BM25 and merged by Reciprocal Rank Fusion.
{
  "query": {
    "multi_match": {
      "query": "running shoes",
      "fields": ["title^3", "brand^2", "description"],
      "type": "best_fields"
    }
  },
  "size": 20
}

Worked example. Query "shoe". Doc A: title "Shoe" (len 1), doc B: description with 200 words mentioning shoe once. BM25 gives A a much higher score through length normalization even though TF is equal. If doc C is a sponsored, out-of-stock item, a business rule can demote it with a function score multiplier of 0.1.

Measure quality. Offline: NDCG@10, MRR, precision@k against human-labelled judgments. Online: click-through rate, zero-result rate, add-to-cart rate, A/B tests. Debug with explain API.

Industry examples. Amazon's A9 mixes text match with sales rank; Google uses PageRank-like link signals plus ML; Airbnb applies learning-to-rank on top of Elasticsearch; Etsy and Walmart publish talks on hybrid lexical and vector retrieval.

Decision gravity. Ranking formulas are reversible via config and A/B test (cheap to change). Heavy models raise latency; every 10 ms matters. Personalization adds cache fragmentation.

Everyday analogy. A librarian who finds all books containing your word, then puts first those where it is the title, rare, and popular.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "ranking = keyword count".
  • Ignoring evaluation: no judgment set, no A/B test.
  • Putting an expensive model on all matching docs instead of a rerank of top N.

notes.title: Elasticsearch architecture: nodes, shards, replicas
notes.html:
An Elasticsearch cluster is nodes holding shards of indices; each shard is a self-contained Lucene index.

  • Index: a logical collection (like a table), for example products.
  • Primary shard: a horizontal slice of the index (documents routed by hash(_id) % number_of_primary_shards). The primary count is fixed at creation (can be changed only by split/shrink/reindex).
  • Replica shard: a copy of a primary: failover plus extra read capacity.
  • Node roles: master-eligible (cluster state, elections), data (hold shards; tiers hot/warm/cold), ingest (pipelines), coordinating (route and merge).

Query path is scatter-gather in two phases:

  1. Query phase: coordinator sends the query to one copy of every shard; each returns its top from+size doc ids with scores.
  2. Fetch phase: coordinator merges, picks the global top N, then fetches the full documents from the owning shards.
PUT /products
{
  "settings": { "number_of_shards": 6, "number_of_replicas": 1,
                "refresh_interval": "5s" },
  "mappings": { "properties": {
    "title":  { "type": "text", "analyzer": "english" },
    "brand":  { "type": "keyword" },
    "price":  { "type": "float" },
    "created":{ "type": "date" } } }
}

Near real-time. A new document is searchable after a refresh (default every 1 s), not instantly; it is first in memory, flushed to a segment visible for search. Durability comes from the translog (fsync per request by default or per 5 s with async), then periodic flush/commit to disk. Hence "near real-time search", not real-time.

Sizing rules of thumb (confirm in current docs).

  • Aim for shard sizes of 10 to 50 GB (up to about 50 GB for search; logs often 20 to 40 GB).
  • Keep fewer than about 20 shards per GB of heap on a node.
  • Give Elasticsearch heap at most about 50% of RAM and under about 31 GB (compressed object pointers), rest left for the OS page cache that Lucene relies on.
  • Too many tiny shards waste memory; too few big shards limit parallelism and slow recovery.

Cluster health. green = all shards allocated, yellow = replicas missing, red = a primary is missing. Mapping explosion (dynamic fields from user-controlled JSON keys) and unbounded wildcards cause outages.

Deep pagination. from=10000,size=10 makes each shard produce 10,010 hits; the default cap index.max_result_window = 10,000 prevents this. Use search_after with a sort tiebreaker, or point-in-time (PIT) for deep paging.

Worked example. 600 GB of product data, growth 20%/year. Target 30 GB per shard: 20 primaries, 1 replica = 40 shards, 1.2 TB of disk plus 30% headroom = about 1.6 TB across e.g. 4 data nodes of 500 GB usable disk each.

Decision gravity. Primary shard count is hard to change (one-way-ish); overshard slightly using the index lifecycle and rollover for time-based data. Use aliases (products -> products_v7) so you can reindex behind the scenes and switch with no client change.

Industry examples. Netflix, Uber, GitHub (moved code search to its own Rust-based engine), Wikipedia, and countless observability stacks (ELK/Elastic Stack, OpenSearch at AWS). Time-series logs use data streams with rollover at 50 GB or 1 day.

Everyday analogy. A publisher with several print shops, each holding a part of the catalogue; a customer question goes to all shops, each shop sends its best candidates, a manager picks the overall best.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Elasticsearch is ACID or a source of truth.
  • Setting number_of_shards to 100 "for scale".
  • Deep paging with large offsets.
  • Forgetting refresh delay when a test reads right after write.

notes.title: Indexing pipelines: keeping search in sync
notes.html:
The search index is a derived copy of data that lives in a database; you need a reliable pipeline to keep it updated.

Options:

  1. Dual write from the app (write to DB and to ES). Simple but fragile: if the second write fails, they diverge, and ordering is not guaranteed. Avoid.
  2. Transactional outbox: the app writes the row and an event row in one DB transaction; a relay publishes events to a queue. Reliable.
  3. Change data capture (CDC): Debezium reads the Postgres WAL/MySQL binlog and publishes row changes to Kafka; a consumer indexes them into Elasticsearch. No app changes; handles any writer.
  4. Periodic batch reindex from DB snapshot: simplest, high lag; good for the initial load.

Design points:

  • Idempotent upserts: use the DB primary key as document _id and the row version as version_type=external so late or duplicated events never overwrite newer data.
  • Bulk API: send batches of 1,000 to 5,000 docs (5 to 15 MB) rather than one request per doc; during large loads set refresh_interval: -1 and number_of_replicas: 0, then restore.
  • Backpressure and retries with a dead-letter queue for poison documents (mapping errors).
  • Full reindex without downtime: build products_v8 in the background from a snapshot while consuming the change stream into both indexes, verify counts and sample queries, then flip the alias atomically.
  • Deletes: capture tombstones; otherwise deleted products still appear.
  • Denormalization: search docs embed what they need (brand name, category path) because there are no joins; when a brand is renamed, reindex affected docs.
# Atomically switch the alias after a reindex
curl -XPOST localhost:9200/_aliases -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "actions": [
    {"remove": {"index": "products_v7", "alias": "products"}},
    {"add":    {"index": "products_v8", "alias": "products"}}
  ]}'

Worked example. 5,000 product updates/s peak. Bulk size 2,000 docs: 2.5 bulk requests/s, easy. Pipeline lag budget 5 s: monitor consumer lag in Kafka and the refresh delay; if lag exceeds 30 s, alert because search shows stale price.

Industry examples. Debezium + Kafka + Elasticsearch connector is the standard open-source setup; LinkedIn's Galene and Uber's search infra feed from Kafka streams; Shopify and Etsy rebuild indexes via alias swap.

Decision gravity. CDC/outbox gives decoupling and replay (reversible, correct under failure). Dual write is easy now and expensive later. The alias-swap pattern makes mapping changes routine instead of a crisis.

Everyday analogy. A newspaper archive clerk who receives a notice for every change in the main records office and updates the card catalogue; if the clerk misses a notice, the catalogue lies.

Common interview traps.

  • Dual writes without reconciliation.
  • Not planning for reindexing (mapping change = reindex).
  • Forgetting deletes and out-of-order events.
  • Treating the index as authoritative: always able to rebuild from the source of truth.

notes.title: Search features: autocomplete, typos, facets, scaling
notes.html:
Autocomplete. Use edge n-grams at index time (sho, shoe) or a dedicated completion suggester (FST in memory), plus popularity weighting from query logs. Latency target under 50 ms, so debounce on the client (200 to 300 ms) and cache top prefixes in Redis/CDN.

Typo tolerance. Fuzzy matching via edit distance (Levenshtein): fuzziness: AUTO allows 0 edits for 1-2 chars, 1 edit for 3-5 chars, 2 edits above. Also "did you mean" suggesters and phonetic analyzers.

Facets / aggregations (counts by brand, price buckets) come from doc values: terms and range aggregations. High-cardinality aggregations cost memory.

Filters vs queries. Filters (exact, yes/no) are cached and do not affect scoring; use them for category, in-stock, price range. Put them in bool.filter.

{ "query": { "bool": {
    "must":   { "match": { "title": "running shoes" } },
    "filter": [ { "term": { "brand": "nike" } },
                { "range": { "price": { "lte": 5000 } } } ] } },
  "aggs": { "by_brand": { "terms": { "field": "brand" } } } }

Scaling and operations.

  • Read-heavy: add replicas (each replica adds read capacity and memory need).
  • Write-heavy: more primaries / faster disks (NVMe), bulk indexing, larger refresh intervals.
  • Hot-warm-cold tiers for time-series data; searchable snapshots to object storage for cold data.
  • Protect the cluster: circuit breakers, query timeouts, limit wildcard/regex/script queries, rate limit per tenant.
  • Monitor: query latency p99, rejected thread pool tasks (search, write queues), JVM heap and GC, segment count, pending tasks, disk watermarks (85% low, 90% high, 95% flood stage by default).

Worked example. Black Friday traffic 20x: 500 -> 10,000 queries/s. Each node does about 1,500 queries/s on this index with p99 under 80 ms. Need 7 data nodes holding replicas; with 6 primaries x 1 replica on 4 nodes, raise replicas to 3 (4 copies) and add 4 nodes, plus a cache for the top 1,000 popular queries which absorbs roughly 40% of traffic.

Industry examples. Amazon and Swiggy autocomplete from query logs, GitHub's custom code-search engine, Algolia / Typesense / Meilisearch as managed or lightweight alternatives, Vespa for large-scale ranking, Google and Bing at web scale.

Decision gravity. Managed (OpenSearch Service, Elastic Cloud, Algolia) vs self-hosted: operations cost vs control and bill; reversible but migrations need reindex. Choose Postgres full-text first if data is small and requirements simple.

Everyday analogy. A shop assistant who guesses your word as you start spelling it, forgives your spelling, and shows filters for size and colour.

Common interview traps.

  • Using expensive wildcard queries (*foo*) in production.
  • Forgetting to cache popular queries and autocomplete.
  • Not isolating the search cluster from the main database failures.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Databases cannot do text search at scale; inverted indexes map terms to posting lists.
  • The analyzer (tokenize, normalize, stem, synonyms) must match at index and query time; changing it means reindexing.
  • BM25 ranks by term frequency, rarity and length; production ranking adds boosts, business signals, learning-to-rank and vectors with hybrid retrieval.
  • Elasticsearch = shards (Lucene indexes) plus replicas, scatter-gather queries, near real-time refresh; size shards 10 to 50 GB and use aliases.
  • Keep the index in sync with CDC or outbox, idempotent bulk upserts, and alias swaps for reindexing; the DB stays the source of truth.
  • Add autocomplete, fuzziness, filters, caching and monitoring for production quality.

questions.promptHtml: Why can't we just use WHERE title LIKE '%running shoes%' for product search?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Basic check that you know why B-trees do not help with substring search and what search engines add.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A B-tree sorts whole values, so a leading wildcard cannot use it and the database scans every row. On 50M titles that is seconds. A search engine builds an inverted index from words to documents so lookup is instant, and adds stemming, typo tolerance and relevance ranking, which LIKE has no concept of.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
LIKE '%shoes%'   -> full scan (~5 GB of text, 5 to 20 s)
Inverted index   -> term "shoe" -> posting list [doc ids] (10 to 50 ms)

Beyond speed, LIKE returns an unordered set: no "best match first", no synonyms ("sneakers"), no language handling. Postgres full-text search (tsvector plus a GIN index) is a good first step under a few million documents; it lacks easy horizontal scale, rich relevance tuning and facets. The search engine is a derived copy of data; the database stays the source of truth.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using regex or leading-wildcard LIKE at scale.
  • Treating the search engine as the system of record.
  • Skipping Postgres FTS when data is small.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a trigram index fix LIKE? -> pg_trgm with GIN can accelerate substring search, but still no relevance ranking or distribution.
  2. What does the engine give you beyond speed? -> Analysis (stemming, synonyms), BM25 ranking, facets, fuzziness.
  3. When would you not add Elasticsearch? -> Few documents, simple filters, small team: Postgres FTS avoids a second system and sync pipeline.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "use Elasticsearch". The senior frames the decision by data size, relevance needs and the sync pipeline cost, and notes the DB stays authoritative.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A marketplace's search page timed out at 30 s on 40M rows; moving to an inverted index brought it under 50 ms and let them add facets.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how an inverted index is built and queried, and what Lucene segments are.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests knowledge of the analysis pipeline, posting lists, immutability and merges, which explain every operational behavior of Elasticsearch.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each document is analyzed (tokenize, lowercase, stem, synonyms) and each term maps to a sorted posting list of doc ids with frequencies and positions. A query runs the same analyzer and intersects or unions lists. Lucene writes immutable segments; updates are delete plus insert, and background merges compact segments and drop deleted docs.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Doc1 "red running shoes"  Doc2 "blue running shirt"  Doc3 "red shirt"
red   -> 1,3     run -> 1,2     shoe -> 1     shirt -> 2,3     blue -> 2
"red AND shirt" -> {1,3} intersect {2,3} = {3}

Phrase queries use positions (run at p, shoe at p+1). Sorted lists intersect by merge walk or skip lists; posting lists are delta-encoded and bit-packed. Cost depends on list length: a rare term touches thousands of entries, "the" touches millions. Segments: new docs buffer in memory and flush to a small immutable segment; deletes are bits in a bitset; merges rewrite many segments into fewer. Immutability gives cache-friendliness and lock-free reads, at the cost of write amplification during merges and updates being full re-index of the document. Because tokens are baked in at write time, changing the analyzer needs a full reindex.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Different analyzers at index and query time, then "nothing matches".
  • Believing updates are in place.
  • Overly aggressive stemming that conflates unrelated words.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why are deletes not instant on disk? -> Marked in a bitset, physically removed at merge.
  2. Why do rare terms query faster? -> Shorter posting lists to intersect.
  3. How does autocomplete use this? -> Edge n-grams at index time create prefix terms, so prefix lookup is a normal term lookup.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "word to documents map". The senior ties segments, merges, delete bitsets and analyzer lock-in to operational consequences (disk usage spikes, reindex).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team updated a hot counter field in every document on each view; merge load and segment churn pushed indexing latency up until counters moved to a separate store.

questions.contextHtml:
Search for "Running Shoes" returns 0 hits although documents titled "Nike running shoes" exist. The mapping:

PUT /products
{ "mappings": { "properties": {
    "title": { "type": "keyword" },
    "brand": { "type": "text" } } } }

and the query:

GET /products/_search
{ "query": { "match": { "title": "Running Shoes" } } }

Dev says "the data is there, I can see it in _source". A colleague suggests increasing replicas.
questions.promptHtml: Why no results, and how do you fix it without downtime?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Maybe replicas are not synced." It ignores the mapping and that _source shows the original text, not the indexed tokens.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does exact Nike running shoes as a term query match? Is the field also needed for sorting/aggregations? How many docs?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Query with term on exact title as a stop-gap, or add a title.text subfield and use it in queries once it exists.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: keyword type indexes the whole string as one token with no lowercasing, so "Running Shoes" does not equal "Nike running shoes"; wrong analyzer; stale index.
  4. How I'd verify: GET /products/_analyze with field title and the text; GET /products/_mapping.
  5. Root cause: keyword is for exact values, filters, aggregations. Full-text search needs a text field with an analyzer.
  6. Fix:
"title": { "type": "text", "analyzer": "english",
           "fields": { "raw": { "type": "keyword" } } }

Changing a field type needs a new index and reindex: create products_v2, _reindex, flip the alias. Keep title.raw for sorting and facets. 7. Prevention: Index templates with explicit mappings, dynamic: strict, a relevance smoke test in CI. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use update_by_query hoping to change the type; mapping types are immutable for existing fields. A multi-field costs extra index size, which is acceptable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does brand: text also hurt facets? -> Aggregating on analyzed text needs fielddata (heap-heavy) or a keyword subfield.
  • Search time analyzer different? -> Possible (search_analyzer) for edge n-grams, but must be deliberate.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: dynamic mapping typed a short string field as text and a long-id field as keyword, then autocomplete silently returned nothing for a locale.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames replicas.
  • Hire: spots keyword vs text and reindexes.
  • Strong hire: uses _analyze, multi-fields, alias swap, strict mappings and tests.

questions.contextHtml: Product catalog: 600 GB now, growing 20%/year, plan for 3 years. Query load 800/s peak, p99 target 100 ms. A junior proposes number_of_shards: 100 "so we never have to reshard". Each data node: 64 GB RAM, 1 TB NVMe usable (keep 30% headroom).
questions.promptHtml: Choose shard and node counts and defend them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepts 100 shards ("more is safer") without computing shard size or heap overhead.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it one index or time-based? Update rate? Replica count for availability? Aggregation heavy?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A, planning.
  3. Hypotheses (options): few large shards vs many small ones.
  4. Math: 3-year size = 600 x 1.2^3 = about 1,037 GB. Target 30 GB per shard gives about 35 primaries. 100 shards would be about 10 GB each at the end (6 GB today): many tiny shards, each with fixed heap and file-handle cost and extra work per query (scatter-gather to 100 shards). With 1 replica: 70 shards, about 2.1 TB disk; with 30% headroom roughly 2.7 TB, so 3 nodes of 1 TB is tight; choose 4 data nodes (about 4 TB). Each node holds about 17 to 18 shards, well under the rule of thumb of about 20 shards per GB of heap (heap 31 GB allows hundreds).
  5. Decision: Start with 20 primaries (30 GB each today at 600 GB), 1 replica, 4 nodes; growth to about 50 GB per shard in 3 years is within range. Use aliases so a future reindex to more shards is routine.
  6. Fix (if wrong later): _split or reindex into a new index and swap the alias.
  7. Prevention: Monitor shard size, heap and segment counts; ILM rollover if time-based.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: 100 shards looks scalable but increases query fan-out latency and cluster state; too few shards limit parallelism and recovery speed. Heap at most about 31 GB, the rest for OS page cache.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Traffic grows 4x? -> Add replicas and nodes (read capacity scales with copies), not primaries.
  • One node dies? -> Replicas promote; recovery copies 30 GB shards, fast; this is why we avoid 300 GB shards.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a cluster with 40,000 tiny shards had a cluster-state size so large that master elections took minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: arbitrary shard count.
  • Hire: sizes shards at 10 to 50 GB with arithmetic.
  • Strong hire: includes replicas, headroom, heap and page cache, aliases and growth plan.

questions.promptHtml: How does BM25 rank documents, and how does a production system go beyond it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Relevance is the product; interviewers want to see you can reason about ranking signals and evaluate them, not just say "TF-IDF".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: BM25 scores a match by term frequency with diminishing returns, rarity of the term across the corpus (IDF) and field length normalization. Production adds field boosts, business signals like popularity and stock, a rerank step (learning to rank) on the top few hundred, and often vector search merged with BM25. I measure with NDCG offline and click and conversion in A/B tests.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
score = sum_t IDF(t) * tf*(k1+1) / (tf + k1*(1 - b + b*len/avglen)), defaults k1=1.2, b=0.75.

  • TF saturates: the 10th mention adds little.
  • IDF: "gore-tex" matters, "the" does not.
  • Length norm: a match in a 3-word title beats one in a 3,000-word description.
Retrieve top 1000 with BM25  ->  rerank top 100 with LTR / cross-encoder  ->  business rules

Expensive models only on the top N keeps latency flat. Hybrid retrieval: embeddings with an ANN index (HNSW) plus BM25, merged by Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Debug with the explain API. Evaluate: NDCG@10, MRR on judged queries; online CTR, zero-result rate, add-to-cart.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Ranking is keyword count".
  • No evaluation set or A/B test.
  • Running an expensive model on all matches.
  • Boost weights tuned by gut on three queries.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does b=0 do? -> Turns off length normalization.
  2. Why hybrid with vectors? -> Lexical misses synonyms and intent; vectors miss exact tokens such as SKUs.
  3. How do you prevent popular items always winning? -> Cap the popularity boost, add exploration, evaluate on tail queries.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer recites TF-IDF. The senior describes saturation, normalization, the rerank architecture and how quality is measured.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A retailer boosted sales rank heavily and the top results stopped changing; adding a capped boost and a query-level A/B test restored discovery of new items.

questions.contextHtml: Head of product: "Search is bad. Users say they can't find things. Fix it." The site has 3M products, 80k searches/day. Engineers want to switch to a vector database.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks a technology (vectors, new engine) before defining "bad" or looking at queries.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which queries fail (head vs tail)? What is the zero-result rate and CTR trend? Specific examples? Did something change recently (new analyzer, reindex)? Which business metric: conversion or search exits?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pull the top 200 queries and the top 100 zero-result queries from logs and eyeball them; fix obvious issues (synonyms, spelling, missing stock filter).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: zero-result queries from typos or vocabulary gap; ranking order poor on head queries; stale index (sync lag); wrong field boosts; real semantic gap.
  4. How I'd verify: Build a judgment set of 300 queries with human labels, compute NDCG@10 and zero-result rate as the baseline; use explain on 10 failures; check indexing lag.
  5. Root cause: Usually a mix; typically 60% of complaints are zero-results and synonyms, not the model.
  6. Fix: Synonyms and fuzziness, field boosts, filter out of stock, popularity signal; later LTR or hybrid vectors if the offline gap remains. Ship each change behind an A/B test.
  7. Prevention: Weekly dashboard (zero-result rate, CTR@3, reformulation rate), query regression suite in CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not migrate to a vector database first: it is a large cost and does not fix typos or stale data by itself.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Executives want a result in 2 weeks? -> Synonyms and zero-result fixes are days; ranking models need labels.
  • How big a judgment set? -> A few hundred queries with 10 to 20 labelled results each gives a usable signal; more for tail coverage.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: "search is broken" turned out to be a stuck indexing consumer: prices and stock were 9 hours stale.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: jumps to vectors.
  • Hire: asks for metrics and query logs, proposes baseline.
  • Strong hire: measurement-first plan, ranks hypotheses, A/B ships, includes freshness check.

questions.promptHtml: A document was indexed successfully but a search a moment later does not find it. Why, and how does Elasticsearch keep that document from being lost on a crash?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks understanding of refresh, translog and flush, a common source of flaky tests and wrong claims about consistency.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Elasticsearch is near real-time: a new document sits in an in-memory buffer and becomes searchable only after a refresh creates a new segment, by default every 1 second. Durability is separate: each write is appended to the translog, fsynced per request by default, and periodic flush commits segments to disk. So indexed means durable, not yet searchable.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
index request -> in-memory buffer + translog (fsync)  -> refresh (1s) -> searchable segment
                                                      -> flush/commit -> segments on disk, translog trimmed

On crash, the node replays the translog since the last commit. Replicas receive each operation too; a write is acknowledged after the primary and in-sync replicas apply it. Tuning: during a bulk load set refresh_interval: -1 and number_of_replicas: 0, load, then restore: fewer small segments and merges. ?refresh=wait_for blocks until visible but adds latency; refresh=true on every write hurts throughput. Get by id is real-time (reads the translog), search is not. translog.durability: async trades a few seconds of loss risk for speed.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Tests that index then search immediately without refresh.
  • refresh=true on every request.
  • Calling Elasticsearch ACID.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not refresh every 10 ms? -> Creates many tiny segments, heavy merging and CPU.
  2. What if the translog fsync is async and the node dies? -> You can lose the last few seconds of acknowledged writes; rebuildable from the source of truth.
  3. Why prefer idempotent re-index over relying on ES durability? -> The DB is the authority; the index can always be rebuilt.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "eventual consistency". The senior separates visibility (refresh) from durability (translog), knows the throughput knobs and treats the index as rebuildable.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout confirmation page searched orders right after creation and showed "not found" 1 in 20 times until it read from the DB by id instead.

questions.contextHtml:
A SEO crawler and an "export results" feature page deep through results using from/size. Alert: search p99 from 80 ms to 6 s, JVM heap 92%, GC pauses 4 s. Index: 24 primary shards, 1 replica.

GET /products/_search?from=90000&size=100   took: 5400
circuit_breaking_exception: [parent] Data too large, data for [<search>] would be larger than limit
rejected search tasks: 3,100 in 5 min

Normal traffic is unchanged. Another team suspects "too many new products".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add nodes." Deep pagination cost grows with offset times shards; more nodes does not remove it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which clients send large from? Did index.max_result_window get raised from the default 10,000? Who deployed the export feature?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Block or rate limit the crawler by user-agent/IP, lower max_result_window back to 10,000, cap from+size at the API layer.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: deep from (each of 24 shards builds and returns 90,100 hits to the coordinator, merging 2.16M entries per request); crawler concurrency; fielddata or aggregations; GC from large queries.
  4. How I'd verify: Slow log (index.search.slowlog), _tasks?detailed, request logs filtered by from>10000.
  5. Root cause: Each shard must collect top from+size entries; the coordinator merges shards x (from+size). 24 x 90,100 = 2.16M candidates for 100 results, memory heavy and repeated per page.
  6. Fix: Use search_after with a unique sort tiebreaker (for example [_score, id]) and a point-in-time (PIT) for a stable view; for exports use scroll or PIT with search_after, or a batch job from the DB/Parquet snapshot instead of the search cluster. Cap UI paging (users rarely go beyond page 10).
  7. Prevention: API limit on page depth, query timeouts, per-tenant rate limits, slow log alerts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not raise max_result_window (it hides the problem and risks OOM). search_after loses random access to "page 500"; acceptable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Users need "jump to page 40"? -> Cap at the result window and encourage filters; or compute a cursor per page.
  • Does PIT cost anything? -> It holds segments open (disk and heap) until it expires; keep keepalive short.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a bot paginated 5,000 pages a minute and the first symptom was GC pauses, not CPU.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds nodes or heap.
  • Hire: search_after, caps, blocks crawler.
  • Strong hire: explains shards x (from+size) math, PIT, alternative export path and guardrails.

questions.contextHtml: An e-commerce app dual-writes: save product in Postgres, then call Elasticsearch index. Incident: prices changed to Rs 999 in Postgres but search showed old Rs 1,999 for 6 hours for ~12,000 products; customers saw the wrong price in listings. Logs: ES had a 4-minute brownout; app swallowed the exception (catch (Exception e) { log.warn(...) }). A second symptom: two quick updates arrived at ES out of order for some SKUs. Peak rate 5,000 updates/s.
questions.promptHtml: Write the post-incident review and the target design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add retries around the ES call." Retries still reorder and do not cover process crashes after the DB commit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are there other writers to the DB (admin scripts, batch)? Is delete handled? What staleness is acceptable (5 s)? Can we replay from the DB?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Re-index the affected SKUs from Postgres (bulk) and show price from the DB on product pages as the source of truth for checkout.
  3. Hypotheses (root causes), ranked: dual write with no atomicity (DB commit succeeded, index call failed and exception swallowed); no ordering or versioning (older update arrived later); no reconciliation job; no lag alerting.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare updated_at in DB vs _source in ES for a sample; count mismatches with a scan job.
  5. Root cause: Two systems updated by the app with no shared transaction; failure between the two writes is silent and permanent.
  6. Fix: Transactional outbox (write row + event in one DB transaction) or CDC with Debezium reading the WAL into Kafka; an indexer consumes with idempotent upserts: document _id = primary key, version_type=external using the row version so older events are rejected. Bulk batches of 1,000 to 5,000 docs (2.5 bulk requests/s at 5,000 updates/s), DLQ for poison docs, capture deletes as tombstones.
Postgres --WAL--> Debezium --> Kafka --> Indexer (bulk, external version) --> Elasticsearch
  1. Prevention: Alert on consumer lag above 30 s, a nightly reconciliation of counts and checksums by sampled keys, a replay runbook, price shown in checkout always read from the DB.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: CDC adds Kafka and Debezium to operate; outbox needs app changes but keeps events explicit. I would not rely on "refresh and hope". Seconds of staleness is the accepted contract.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A brand is renamed, affecting 200k docs? -> Denormalized field: emit update events or run a controlled reindex of affected docs at lower priority.
  • Poison message blocks the partition? -> DLQ after N retries and alert.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a silent catch-and-log on index calls hid a mapping error; 3% of products never appeared in search for two months.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: retries only.
  • Hire: outbox or CDC with idempotent upserts.
  • Strong hire: external versioning, deletes, DLQ, lag alerting, reconciliation and replay.

questions.contextHtml: You need to add an edge n-gram analyzer for autocomplete and change the language analyzer, on products_v7: 80M documents, 700 GB, 6,000 updates/s peak, search traffic 1,500 QPS that cannot be interrupted. Cluster has 25% free capacity. Change window: no downtime allowed.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Update the mapping in place." Analyzer changes on existing fields are not allowed; and a blind reindex loses updates written during the copy.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the app using an alias or the index name? Do we have a replayable change stream (Kafka) or only the DB? Acceptable extra load during migration? Rollback window?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident, but first confirm there is an alias products pointing to products_v7.
  3. Hypotheses (approaches): _reindex from v7 to v8 (reads from the live index; picks up changes only up to a point); rebuild from the DB snapshot plus replay stream; reindex with dual-consume.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare doc counts and a sample of 1,000 queries between v7 and v8 (overlap@10, NDCG on judgments), diff _source for random IDs.
  5. Plan: (a) Create products_v8 with new settings, refresh_interval: -1, replicas: 0. (b) Record the Kafka offset T0, bulk load from a snapshot or _reindex with throttling (requests_per_second) to protect search latency. (c) Start a second consumer group writing the change stream from offset T0 into v8 (external versioning makes replay idempotent). (d) When lag is near zero, restore replicas and refresh. (e) Verify counts and relevance. (f) Atomically swap the alias with _aliases remove/add; keep v7 for 24 to 72 hours for rollback and keep dual-writing. (g) Delete v7.
curl -XPOST localhost:9200/_aliases -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
 "actions":[{"remove":{"index":"products_v7","alias":"products"}},
            {"add":{"index":"products_v8","alias":"products"}}]}'
  1. Fix (capacity): Disk: v8 needs 700 GB x (1 + replicas) extra; with 25% headroom check watermarks (85/90/95%) before starting. Temporarily scale out data nodes.
  2. Prevention: Make this a routine, scripted runbook; keep mappings in code; alias-only access from apps.
  3. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not reindex at full speed in business hours (query p99 suffers); I would not skip the change-stream replay (silent drift).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Deletes during the copy? -> Replay tombstones with versions; reconcile with a final diff of IDs.
  • Rollback after the swap? -> Flip the alias back; v7 stays fed by the dual consumer during the grace period.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team reindexed with _reindex only, flipped the alias, and discovered 40k updates written mid-copy were missing for a week.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: in-place change.
  • Hire: new index plus alias swap.
  • Strong hire: replay stream, throttling, validation by relevance metrics, disk watermarks, rollback.

questions.contextHtml: Sale event in 3 weeks: expected search traffic 20x, from 500 to 10,000 QPS, autocomplete adds about 3x requests per search session. Cluster: 6 primaries, 1 replica, 4 data nodes; each node handles about 1,500 QPS at p99 under 80 ms for this index. Today CPU is 35% at peak. Top 1,000 queries are about 40% of traffic.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more nodes until it works" with no per-node capacity model, cache, or load test.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is 10,000 QPS search only or including autocomplete? Staleness tolerance for cached results? Budget? Is query mix cache-friendly?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A, planning; start with a load test replay of production queries at 2x.
  3. Hypotheses (levers): replicas (read capacity), caching popular queries and autocomplete prefixes, expensive-query reduction, bigger nodes.
  4. Math: Autocomplete may add 3 x 10,000 = 30,000 prefix queries, but 95% hit a Redis/CDN prefix cache (top prefixes are hot), leaving about 1,500 QPS. Search: 10,000 QPS with a result cache absorbing 40% leaves 6,000 QPS for ES. At 1,500 QPS per node per copy-set... one full copy of data (6 primaries) answers the query with all its shards, so capacity depends on copies: 4 nodes handle 6,000 QPS only if each query's work spreads; with 4 copies (replicas=3) spread over 8 nodes we have about 8 x 1,500 = 12,000 QPS theoretical, 2x headroom over 6,000.
  5. Plan: replicas 1 to 2 (3 copies of each shard, 18 shards on 6 nodes), add 2 data nodes (warm up caches by routing shadow traffic), set search.max_buckets and query timeouts, rate limit per client, disable heavy aggregations or script queries during the event, separate autocomplete onto its own small index/cluster so it cannot starve search.
  6. Fix (degradation plan): Feature flags to turn off facets, fuzziness and personalization; serve stale cache on overload.
  7. Prevention: Load test at 1.5x target with the real query distribution; dashboard on p99, rejected search thread pool tasks, heap, GC.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Each extra replica adds a full copy of data (disk) and write work; I would not scale up primaries for a read surge. Cache raises staleness (price changes): TTL 30 s.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Data nodes take 30 minutes to recover shards when scaling? -> Pre-scale a week early and avoid shard-allocation storms (throttle recoveries).
  • Cache stampede on a popular query? -> Request coalescing and jittered TTL.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: autocomplete queries sharing the main cluster consumed the search thread pool and caused main search rejections; isolating it solved the next sale.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "add nodes".
  • Hire: replicas, caching, load test.
  • Strong hire: separated autocomplete, per-node capacity math, graceful degradation, protecting the cluster.

questions.contextHtml: A B2B SaaS app has 3M documents (average 5 KB, 15 GB), 150 QPS, text search with filters by tenant and a few facets. Team of 6 backend engineers, no one has operated Elasticsearch. Already running Postgres 15 on managed RDS. The CTO is deciding between Postgres full-text, self-managed Elasticsearch, managed Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, or Algolia. Budget: modest.
questions.promptHtml: Recommend one and say what would make you change your mind.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Elasticsearch is the industry standard." It ignores the team's capacity and the sync pipeline cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Relevance requirements (typos, synonyms, multi-language)? Growth projection? Freshness needs? Multi-tenant isolation? Need for vector or semantic search later?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; decision.
  3. Hypotheses (options) and cost: Postgres FTS: no new system, transactional consistency, GIN index on 15 GB is trivial, weaker relevance tuning and facets at scale. Self-managed ES: powerful but operations (shards, heap, upgrades) for 6 people. Managed OpenSearch/Elastic Cloud: removes most ops, still needs a sync pipeline and monthly bill. Algolia: best typo/autocomplete UX, priced by records and requests (verify pricing), vendor lock-in.
  4. How I'd verify: Prototype 200 real queries on Postgres FTS (tsvector, ts_rank, pg_trgm for typos) and measure p99 and quality; check facet counts query cost.
  5. Recommendation: Start with Postgres FTS plus pg_trgm and a read replica. 15 GB and 150 QPS is within its reach, no sync pipeline, no dual-write bugs, one backup story. Define upgrade triggers: p99 above 200 ms after tuning, need for typo tolerance and autocomplete at quality, vector hybrid, more than about 20 to 30M docs, or relevance team demands.
  6. Fix (the upgrade path): Hide search behind a SearchService interface; build the outbox now so adding an index later is a consumer, not a rewrite; move to managed OpenSearch when triggers hit.
  7. Prevention: Track relevance metrics and latency so triggers are measured.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: This is a reversible decision if the interface and outbox exist; I would not run self-managed Elasticsearch for this team. I would not skip measuring: if the prototype shows poor relevance, go managed search.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Customers demand typo tolerance and instant autocomplete? -> Trigger to managed OpenSearch or Algolia.
  • Tenant data isolation? -> Filter by tenant in all stores; for strict isolation, separate indices or per-tenant partitions.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a small team adopted self-managed Elasticsearch for 2M documents and spent more engineer-weeks on cluster upgrades than on search features.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Elasticsearch by default.
  • Hire: weighs Postgres FTS vs managed options with team and scale in mind.
  • Strong hire: prototype-driven, explicit upgrade triggers, abstraction and outbox for reversibility.
